extracted.intended_audience: patent agents, patent attorneys, patent drafters, and inventors (Philippines-focused guidance, but many rules are general)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting patent claims: required sentence/format conventions, claim parts (preamble/transitional/body), punctuation and antecedent-basis rules, claim-set structure (independent/dependent), special claim types (Jepson, means-plus-function, two‑part, apparatus/method/composition/software/etc.), and jurisdictional notes relevant to the Philippines (IPPHL/Rule 416) and general practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim sentence format
rubrics_metrics.description: WRITTEN AS A SINGLE SENTENCE; CLAIMS IDENTIFIER preceding the sentence, e.g. 'Claim 1'; HEAVILY PUNCTUATED SINGLE SENTENCE AND ENDS WITH A PERIOD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should be single, heavily punctuated sentences and labeled (e.g., 'Claim 1'). Ensure the sentence ends with a period. Place claims toward the end of the issued patent or patent application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of claims in document
rubrics_metrics.description: APPEARS TOWARDS THE END OF THE ISSUED PATENT OR PATENT APPLICATION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are normally located near the end of the patent document or application specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of a claim — overall structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim comprises: a. THE PREAMBLE; b. TRANSITIONAL PHRASE; c. THE BODY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All claims should be drafted with these three parts in mind; each part has distinct functions and wording conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble: identify category and be consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifies the category of the invention e.g., an apparatus, device, article, composition, a method or process. Keep it consistent with the title of the invention. May recite an object of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble wording should match the invention's title and may state the object (e.g., 'AN APPARATUS FOR COOKING', 'A METHOD FOR MAKING TEA', 'A COMPOSITION FOR TREATING MALARIA'). Example variations show specificity: 'AN APPARATUS FOR COOKING GRAINS' vs 'A METHOD FOR MAKING WARM BEVERAGES'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase — open-ended 'comprising'
rubrics_metrics.description: OPEN-ENDED PHRASE (comprising) — 'including', 'containing', 'characterized by' — do not exclude any additional unrecited elements — expand the scope of the claim by allowing for other elements or limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'comprising' or similar open terms when you intend to allow additional, unrecited components; example format: 'An apparatus, comprising: element1; element2; and element3.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase — closed 'consisting of'
rubrics_metrics.description: CLOSED PHRASE (consisting of) — limits the scope of the claim to nothing more than the specifically recited elements — claim covers only elements named and nothing more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'consisting of' to exclude any additional elements. For compositions, percentages should add up to 100% when using 'consisting of' (example chemical compound consisting of 50% A; 25% B; 25% C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of the claim — elements and relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Must recite elements and limitation of the Claim. Explains how the different elements exist in relationship to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not merely catalog parts; show how elements are connected or interact. Example contrasting weak vs proper body: 'four legs; 16 screws; and a top.' (mere list) versus 'a head portion connected to the handle; and a protrusion being secured to the handle.' (shows relationships).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere part lists — require linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: NOT merely a list of parts/cataloging of parts — Must be connected in some manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting, ensure elements are linked (e.g., 'head portion connected to the handle'), not just enumerated without relational language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement (Jepson) type claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Preamble – statement of the most relevant prior art. Transitional Phrase – 'wherein the improvement comprises'. The body – provides the novel feature/s of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this format to highlight improvements over cited prior art. Example: 'A game device having [prior art elements], wherein the improvement comprises a protrusion being secured to the handle.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Two‑part form claims (Rule 416, Philippines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-part form adopted in the Philippines: (1) designation of the subject matter — the general technical class and the technical features necessary for the definition and that are part of prior art; and (2) a characterizing portion preceded by 'characterized in that' stating the technical features to be protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Rule 416 for two-part claims in the Philippines. Example: 'A game device, comprising a handle and a head portion connected to the handle, characterized in that, a protrusion is secured to the handle.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Means‑plus‑function claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Recite function performed by structures disclosed in the specification instead of specifically defined structures. Interpretation varies from jurisdiction to jurisdiction. The means‑plus‑function clauses recited in the claim must be adequately described by the structure carrying the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using 'means for ...' ensure the specification discloses corresponding structure to avoid indefiniteness; jurisdictional interpretation differs, so check local law. Example: 'a means for holding rice; and a heater configured to heat the rice-holding means.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim punctuation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma separates the preamble from the transitional phrase. A colon separates the transitional phrase from the body. The small paragraphs that define and describe the logical elements are separated with semi colons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow punctuation rules to improve clarity and conform to practice: Preamble, transitional phrase: Element (#1); Element (#2); and Element (#3). Use colon after 'comprising:' and semicolons between elements; use commas appropriately before transitional/characterizing clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements in the patent claim must have correct antecedent basis. Use indefinite article 'a' or 'an' when introducing an element for the first time. Use definite article 'the' or 'said' when referring back to the introduced element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce elements with 'a'/'an' and refer back with 'the'/'said' to maintain clear antecedent basis. Example: first: 'a handle ... an anti-slippage means is secured to the handle.' improved: 'a handle ... connected to said handle ... an anti-slippage means is secured to said handle.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference numerals and bracket expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may include reference numerals and bracket expressions (e.g., An apparatus (10), comprising: a plurality of printed pages (11); a binding (12)... ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference numerals may be used to link claim elements to drawings but are not substitute limitations. Bracketed numerals can clarify correspondence to figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special claim phrases to define structure or function
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of special words such as 'wherein', 'whereby', 'such that' to further define a structure or provide a function associated with a given structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these clauses to add functional or relational limitations (e.g., 'a cover attached to the binding, wherein the cover is detachable from the binding'). Place such clauses appropriately (often after a comma or characterizing phrase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple elements requirement (minimum elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many patent offices including the IPPHL require claims to recite at least two elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid single-element claims in jurisdictions that require multiple elements; provide at least two elements (e.g., processor and memory) unless a single-element claim is permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent claim characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: INDEPENDENT CLAIM — BROADEST CLAIM. STAND ALONE AND DOES NOT NEED A LIMITATION FROM ANOTHER CLAIM IN ORDER TO BE COMPLETE. PATENT APPLICATION MAY HAVE MORE THAN ONE (1) INDEPENDENT CLAIM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft independent claims to capture the broadest inventive concept while remaining supportable in the specification. It's acceptable to have multiple independent claims directed to different aspects (apparatus, method, composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claim characteristics and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: DEPENDENT CLAIM — DEPENDS ON ANOTHER (EITHER AN INDEPENDENT CLAIM OR DEPENDENT CLAIM). MUST NOT EXTEND THE SCOPE OF THE PROTECTION OF THE INVENTION DEFINED IN THE INDEPENDENT CLAIM/S. 'FALL BACK' DURING EXAMINATION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims should add limitations narrowing an independent claim and provide fallback positions during prosecution. Ensure dependency language correctly references the claim(s) relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus claim specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparatus Claims — Protect an apparatus or device. Recite in the preamble what the apparatus 'is' and/or 'what it does'. Recite in the claim's body the essential inventive elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure apparatus claims with a clear preamble and body reciting the inventive elements and their relationships (example: camera support with pivotal mounting and legs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method claim specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Method Claims — Recite a sequence of steps that complete a task or accomplish a result. Active Steps may be recited in order of performance, but are usually interpreted as being performed in any order unless otherwise specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If step order is critical, state it explicitly; otherwise courts/offices may treat steps as order-independent. Example method claim enumerates boiling water; adding sugar; adding tea leaves; filtering; adding milk.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Use' claims and jurisdictional limits
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Use' Claims — Similar to method claims. May be interpreted as method claims. Not allowed in all jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'use' claims (including Swiss‑type claims for second medical use) when appropriate, but verify local law — not all patent offices permit pure 'use' claim formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second medical-use (Swiss‑type) claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Second Medical 'Use' Claims — Helpful when substance is already known in the art; example: 'The use of compound XYZ in the manufacture of a treatment for malaria.' Not all jurisdictions permit such types of claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft second medical use (Swiss-type) claims when discovering a new therapeutic use of a known compound; check whether the target jurisdiction recognizes this claim form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition claim specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition claim — Used where claimed invention pertains to the chemical nature of the materials or components used. Claims a 'thing' like a device claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recite components and, where needed, their relative amounts or ranges. Example electroplating solution listing components and amounts (grams per liter, pH-modifying substrate quantities). Consider using 'comprising' vs 'consisting of' depending on scope intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product‑by‑process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Product-by-Process Claims — Claims a product defined in terms of a process of manufacture. Some jurisdictions treat as product claims; other jurisdictions treat as method claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that claiming a product-by-process is the best approach for protection; consequences for patentability/enforceability vary by jurisdiction. Example: 'A metallic salt obtained by a process comprising the steps of ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biotechnology claims and deposits
rubrics_metrics.description: Biotechnology Claim — Relates to practical/commercial/therapeutic uses of living organisms; may include cDNA, recombinant DNA, DNA fragments, proteins, monoclonal antibodies, antisense DNA/RNA, vectors, expression vectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When biological material is involved and deposited, claim the deposited material with accession details as appropriate (example: seed of cotton cultivar designated ... deposited under ATCC Accession No. PTA-5666). Be aware of deposit rules (Budapest Treaty) for international recognition of deposits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposited material and the Budapest Treaty
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an invention involves a biological material, and the material has been deposited, then the patent agent may often claim the material deposited. The Budapest Treaty requires signatory countries to recognize a deposit with any depository approved by WIPO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include deposit accession numbers in claims/specification and confirm the depository is WIPO-approved to ensure cross-jurisdictional recognition under the Budapest Treaty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software claim formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Software Claims — Used where the claimed invention pertains to computer software and/or hardware. Can use device and method claims to cover software inventions. Can also use specialized claim formats to provide an additional scope of protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider multiple claim formats (apparatus, method, computer-readable medium, data structure) to maximize protection. Draft claims to avoid purely abstract formulations where local law requires technical character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer‑readable medium claim format
rubrics_metrics.description: Software claim type — 'computer readable media' format: 'A computer-readable storage medium storing instructions that when executed by a computer cause the computer to perform a method for using a computer system to [a specified function], the method comprising: [list the inventive method steps].'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this format to claim software implemented inventions in a tangible medium. Ensure the claimed instructions map to inventive technical steps disclosed in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data structure claim format
rubrics_metrics.description: Software claim type — 'data structure' format: 'A memory for storing data for access by an application program being executed on a data processing system, comprising: a data structure stored in the memory, the data structure including information resident in a database used by the application program and including: a first data object configured to … a second data object configured to …; and a third data object configured to ….','
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use data-structure style claims to claim particular data arrangements or schemas that embody inventive aspects; recite relationships and configurations of data objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omnibus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Omnibus Claims — Refer to the description or the drawings without providing any specific limitations. Examples: 'An apparatus for harvesting corn as described in the description.' 'A juice machine as shown in Figure 4.' Not all patent offices allow omnibus claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omnibus claims are simple but their acceptability varies by office; include an omnibus claim where possible but base prosecution strategy primarily on other claim types that define clear technical limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design claims — limitation on number
rubrics_metrics.description: Design claim — Only one claim is typically permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For design patents/registrations, draft a single claim to the ornamental design (e.g., 'The ornamental design for an umbrella substantially as shown.'). Include appropriate figures.
